utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Please call the case. We start in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Andrew Cayley and Nicholas Koumjian appearing for the Office of the Prosecutor. Case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we continue with Dr. Donia, please allow me to touch upon some more or less technical issues. Yesterday, the decision on the request of the Office of the Prosecutor was read out but was read out in closed session. As I understood correctly, you want to make use of this, and therefore it's better if there are no objections to have this part of the transcript treated as read out in open session. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objections. Then therefore may it be the part of the transcript of the hearing yesterday shall be treated as read out in open session. Then, not to forget, what about the two videocassettes, one went to the Office of the Prosecutor and one not yet available for the Bench. Is it available, the other -- the first videoclip we saw yesterday, is it available for the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the first one, which has been shown. I think that the Prosecution has better data, but I think the first one hasn't been given to us yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It was disclosed. I believe one had an exhibit number and one did not. It was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The first one didn't have an exhibit number under 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It was disclosed, is my understanding, on the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe that's why we couldn't check. We'll check again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And we will have copies at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then for our proceedings, the following -- hopefully you will agree -- that whenever it's possible, it's better for all of us, and of course the witnesses if we can have the hearings conducted in the morning session. Therefore, on this Friday, I was informed that in all likelihood, Trial Chamber 3 will not sit in this courtroom. And therefore my suggestion is if possible, we should start at 9.00 and close at 1.45. Any objections? We'll come back to this when we have found out whether or not it's possible from the registry. And the same is true next week, from 1 May to May 3. There will be no hearing in Trial Chamber III, and therefore, my intention is to proceed on the three days from 9.00 to 12.30, and from 2.00 to 4.30. I can't see any objections. Over here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just point out we scheduled our witnesses travel on the presumption of having slightly less time, although generally we have found the witnesses take longer than we anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Quite clear about -- just in case. We never know. We have had this experience with Witness A, that indeed it took us one day longer. So we have time enough. And the last question is until now, it was scheduled that on Friday, 31 May, there should be no trial. The intention is to exchange this so-called day without trial against Monday, the 3rd of June, to have the hearing -- this would be the result on Friday, in the morning, but not on Monday in the afternoon. I can't see any objections. I have to come back to this when we have the confirmation of the registry. Thank you. Then we can, I believe, proceed with Dr. Donia, and we could then come immediately to the cross-examinations, if there aren't any other points to be discussed. Then Dr. Donia will be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for not mentioning it earlier. But Your Honour last week asked about a current status of the witness list. One is prepared. I don't know if Your Honour wants that formally filed or just a copy of the latest list given to Your Honours' staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I appreciate the most informal way, because it's the most direct and effective way. And if also the Defence is informed at the same time, no problem. But -- sorry, this brings me to the question, what about the list of 92 bis and the motion on 92 bis witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This list includes that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This list includes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The list that will be provided indicates which witnesses are going to request 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that therefore should already be regarded as your request to take the testimony from these witnesses on the basis of 92 bis. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct. Perhaps I could get together with the Defence counsel and see if there's any objections, and if there is, we can file more formal motions regarding that. If they don't have an objection, then perhaps we can just do it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And of course we are prepared, especially during the next week, when probably we have some additional time to go through witness by witness and then discuss the appropriate decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And, just for Your Honours information, we did give the list this afternoon to the Defence, so they have a copy already of the latest order of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And I don't, additionally not forget, because probably you need the assistance of Dr. Donia for this, that we want to go through at the end of the day the entire so-called SK list, whether or not, it should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My understanding at the time was that you were concerned about the amount of translation in particular that had to be done of the newspaper articles. And in the interim, I have instructed Dr. Donia to go through all of those newspaper articles and highlight the sections in each that need translation. So we will ask for all of these documents to be admitted into evidence, but only portions of the newspaper articles will be translated into the English language unless my learned friends opposite have any additional requirements for translation. All of the minutes, the sort of voluminous book of minutes, all of that has already been translated and we would want all of that admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, then my suggestion that is we don't excuse Dr. Donia before we went through these portions with his assistance in order to avoid translation. Let's do it here in courtroom with his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you wish, Your Honour. I think that may take some considerable time. I have to be honest with you. If he were to, at the end of the proceedings, present you with his marked copy, you would see that actually it drastically reduces amount the translation. I mean, drastically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's find out. Let's go through at the end of the day in the presence of Dr. Donia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Donia. You already have some experience with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Donia. Cross-examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you a series of questions on the report you authorized and submitted, namely Exhibit 42 as it's been commonly referred to here. Sir, can you tell me first perhaps to clean up some items that I missed or I didn't understand the testimony that you gave. When did you complete your report, Exhibit 42?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact date. It was about four weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So approximately March 22nd, 24th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Perhaps a little bit earlier, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also submitted a report it was tendered as evidence in another case called the "OTP against Brdjanin and Talic," and it's an exhibit to some of the materials that you provided us here. And it has, for Your Honours, the Exhibit Number 43. Within that exhibit, you have your curriculum vitae, correct, attached?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, already in the beginning. We decided the last time in your absence that it would be preferable in order to -- to have a good readability of the document, when you are quoting, then please quote page of the transcript precisely. So when you, for example, make reference to the CV of Dr. Donia, if you could at the same time indicate on the page of the transcript. This would facilitate for later readings. I don't hope in the appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can start again, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 43 that is attached to the volumes that I believe everyone has from item number 1 through 50 as far as I can tell, that exhibit 43 is a report that you prepared in the Brdjanin-Talic case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as part of that exhibit, although there's no page number, included in that or attached thereto is your curriculum vitae. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's towards the end of that document, Exhibit 43. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that document, your curriculum vitae is approximately -- or it is actually three and a half pages in length. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour if I may address you on this issue, there no page number on this curriculum vitae, so I'll just go forward if it' okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had testified in the Brdjanin Talic case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you list for us the other cases in which you were a witness for the office of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I was a witness in the Prosecutor -- the Blaskic in 1997. The Prosecutor v Kordic in I think 1999. Perhaps 1998 or 1999. And also in the Bosanski Samac which I believe was in 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the Simic case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I rendered a submission in Prosecutor v Kvocka, the Omarska case, but did not testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think that's -- I'm sorry. I rendered a submission and also testified in the Prosecutor v Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the -- if I may ask you what the ethnic makeup is of the defendants in the Blaskic case that you testified in July of 1997?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The defendant is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the Kordic case? Is it Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July of 1999.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, and those defendants are both Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: In that, and I think all the other cases, the defendants are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Kvocka, Simic, Brdjanin-Talic, and obviously in this case, the ethnic makeup of the defendants are Serbian. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever asked by the office of the Prosecutor to give testimony or to review in connection with a defendant of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your profession, if I understand it, is that of a historian. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you received your PhD. in history, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, in 1976.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your work history since your PhD. in history from 1976 to 1998 I believe was primarily with Merrill Lynch. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: From 1981 to 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your CV, it says that in the year 2000, that you were still working with Merrill Lynch. So is it in 1998 that you quit Merrill Lynch or 2000?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I continued to receive deferred compensation for a period of about two years. So I was technically in the employ of Merrill Lynch, until I believe, August of the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were employed where, in La Jolla, California during that time period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, I was employed in La Jolla, California from July of 1995 until 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told me that from 1981, you started at Merrill Lynch. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't work for Merrill Lynch in the capacity of a historian, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Far from it, as could be imaginable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just want to make sure. From 1981 through 1998 or 2000, whichever date you prefer, is it true that, in fact, primarily your employment involved with Merrill Lynch had nothing to do with the history in any region of the world?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were a full-time employee during that entire period. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than being a historian and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I was resident vice-president, which meant branch office manager.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That dealt with what, purchase and sales of securities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: My job was the management of offices in which other individuals did purchases and sales of securities for clients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the time that you spent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the history -- pardon me. There's a request. I guess I should...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Donia. I'm sorry. Going back to the fact that you testified, sir, in cases against Croats and Serbs and not against Muslims, is it fair to state that you are not rendering an opinion, and have not never rendered an opinion, that there was no atrocities committed by Muslims against the Serbs or Muslims against the Croats during the period of your studies, namely 1991 through 1998?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The question had a negative there. I'm not sure I'm clear on exactly what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object here. It's an extremely convoluted question and actually has a double negative in it. You have not never rendered an opinion. Can you simplify the question so the answer is given actually reflects what is in a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'll withdraw the question and ask it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to state that you are not rendering an opinion that there were no atrocities committed by Muslims against the Serbs during the time period in which you performed your studies in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No. I believe I have rendered in at least one of these, probably two or three of these submissions, the view that atrocities against Serbs were committed by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us in defining the time period that that may have occurred based upon your review and your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, the events to which I referred were in the first months of the war in Sarajevo. I believe May and June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And similarly, do you have an opinion as to whether there have been any atrocities committed by the Muslims against the Croatians during that time period that you just referenced, namely 1991 through 1995, if you will?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That there were such atrocities committed in central Bosnia during the period 1993 inter alia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about prior to 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't believe I have asserted in any report that such atrocities were committed by Muslims prior to 1993 in the period 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By recognising that you haven't asserted it in your report, but based on your review of the materials and your visit to the area or region, and all the work that you've done to compile these reports that we have before us, have you come to any conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: As far as Muslim atrocities committed by Muslims against Croats, I would say that those were principally in the period 1993 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that you're a historian. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'd like to spend a couple minutes trying to distinguish a historian from other practices and studies. Is it true, sir, that you are not a political scientist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, sir, that you are not a military expert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, sir, that you are not a governmental affairs expert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, sir, that you are not a constitutional lawyer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time in which you were asked to give this addendum report in the OTP versus Stakic matter, did you review any statements from witnesses or prospective or potential witnesses that is the Office of the Prosecution would call?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask to review any such statements?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, I did not. I made a general request of relevant documentation that would be helpful in discharging the task I was asked to undertake. But I did not make a specific request for witness summaries, nor for testimony in prior cases regarding the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where I believe you've written about obviously, is there an area called Donja and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's an area in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well I think at least Donja Vakuf is the name of a municipality, and Donja Vakuf is also the name of a town, and Gornji Vakuf is also a name of a town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All within the Vakuf municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No. Donja Vakuf is a municipality. I just don't recall if there's a Gornji Vakuf municipality, but there's no Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipalities you're talking about in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were 109 such municipalities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: In the period 1990, 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. And in the period of 1990, 1991, the Donja Vakuf municipality existed did it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it predominantly a Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know without looking at the population figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you spell that for me, if you don't mind, Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The Vakuf is spelled V-A-K-U-F.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's actually an Arabic or Turkish word. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The word as I understand is a Serbo-Croatian word that is an adaptation of an originally Arabic word which is spelled W-A-Q-A-F, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you state or you set forth in your curriculum vitae on page 4, the last page of your CV, that you're affiliated with a foundation called "Donja Vakuf foundation." Are you familiar with that foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you're the president of the foundation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first name, Donja, that would be you, Dr. Donia, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a Mr. Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: There is to my knowledge no Mr. Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it, sir, that as you sit here, not having testified in any cases against any Muslims, having formed a foundation with the name Vakuf in it, how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, it was a pun on the name of the municipality, Donja Vakuf. We had to add the word "foundation" to be clear what it was. But that's the origin of the name that was given to the foundation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say pun, you weren't making fun of that municipality, were you, in any way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say pun?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The word similarity was very close between the name of that municipality and my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what does this foundation do, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: It is a family foundation. And under U.S. Tax law, that means that monies can be donated to the foundation as tax deductible, but the distributions can only go to other 501 C3 organisations. That is, charity at charitably qualified organisations such as universities, churches, Red Cross, any such qualified charitable foundations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from time to time -- strike that. When was this foundation first started?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe in 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right about the time that you first got involved as a witness testifying for the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think it was a bit before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on your CV, after having reviewed it, is it fair to say that you are not a tenured professor at any of the two universities in which you state you are currently employed by?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct. It's fair to say, and I am not a tenured professor at either place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you are not really employed by those two universities, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I have nominal appointments from them. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not employed by them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't get paid by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a full tenured professor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you currently an assistant professor anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the last ten years, have you been an assistant professor anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, have you ever reviewed the indictment filed by the Office of the Prosecution against Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, I did review it before I began the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you review it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: January of this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: January 2002, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you review the first, second, third, fourth, or which indictment did you review?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I reviewed the most recent one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January of 2002, which one was it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know which number it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if it has been amended since?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the indictment did you rely on in preparing your addendum for the Prijedor area, namely as reflected on Exhibit S42?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: S42 is my report, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I represent that it is. It is the annex to the report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I did not rely at all on the indictment in preparing that report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- strike that. So it's fair to state that despite the fact that in January 2002, you reviewed the indictment against Dr. Stakic, you did not rely at all on the indictment in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I may, let's talk a little bit about history. And so that I can have the same understanding, you being a historian and I not being one, is the field of history, it's actually a study of activities of groups of people in a certain place, in a certain time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That would be one relatively narrow definition of what historians do. I think it can be the study of individuals. It also can be the study of groups compared across time and place and can entail the study of entire regions or parts of the world, as well as very specific places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll accept your broader definition. Working with that, the method of such studies is to review sources of reliable information. Could you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, and sometimes not so reliable information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me in what circumstances, sir, you would rely on unreliable information as a historian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, not all sources are worthless because they may contain false information. They may illuminate the understanding of a particular individual or group about other events and may, in fact, provide, let's say, kind of an image of that group or person's perception of the world at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Despite the fact that it may be unreliable, historians would rely on such information to stereotype a group of people or individuals. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a historian, sir, is it fair to state that in order to get thoroughness and completeness in the study of history in a particular region such as Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period of time of 1991 through 1995, that the more reliable sources and reliable information you rely on, the more thorough and complete your report would be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think in general, that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The study of history, the two methods that historians I believe, respectfully, such as yourself, analyse material comes from what's known as a primary source and a secondary source. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I would say that distinction has become very fuzzy, to the point of almost being inconsequential over the last several decades of historical inquiry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, do you distinguish at all the sources from which you review documents and materials and examine and analyse those items, do you distinguish them from being primary and secondary sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: As I say, it's sometimes -- it's not really possible to put every source in one category or another. There's something more of a continuum depending on the -- let's say the closeness of the source to its point of origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we speak of the primary source, if you will, are we also indicating that a primary source is the source which must be information that is both reliable and identifiable?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: In general, that's the case. But there are totally fabricated primary sources. And so reliability is a contingent variable in assessing the validity of a source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that, what is it we're looking for in those primary sources of documents? What would constitute a reliable document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, an original letter penned by -- authored by a person, that is verifiably in the hand of that person and done by that person is probably the most ideal primary source. I say its contents may be totally false or they may be extremely reliable, but that's the kind of concept of a primary source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those documents from the individual that you were speaking of in his handwriting, those are reliable if further -- further reliable if they are signed by the individual. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't think that the signature relates to the reliability of the information, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondary sources are less reliable and less identifiable, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me an example of one that a primary source would not be better than a secondary source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, as I have indicated, I don't really accept this dichotomy as particularly meaningful. There are collections of documents which are published which may be produced from archival sources, the reliability of which is much more proven and established than that of a primary source which turns out to be a fabrication of facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no example. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I gave you an example of a collection of published documents which might come from an archive. I would give you multiple examples in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina of documents that were published from the administrators of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the early 20th century, which I regard as highly reliable, based on having seen many thousands of them, and established their value vis-a-vis, say, press reports, memoirs, and other documents which attest to their reliability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I notice, sir, in your addendum report or annex to the report, Exhibit S42, it doesn't set forth, at least from my reading, that you actually reviewed the indictment against Dr. Stakic. Was that an oversight?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No. It was not an oversight. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any other materials other than that which you identify Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in your report, Exhibit S42, and that which you share with us today, are there any other documents or materials or data that you relied upon in preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: There are a whole host of documents which I would view as general background reports or information which I've probably gathered, read, and assimilated over the past 25 years. I think that the notations that I have provided in the report give the source for the specific information that I've included in the report. But it's almost impossible to give you a list of all the things that I would use to approximately judge the, let's say, plausibility, of a certain patterns or observations made in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have a binder in front of you that has materials, Exhibits. I believe they are marked SK 1 through SK 41 near you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to your analysis and review of documents, would this binder -- and I also would add, the materials that were provided by counsel during your direct examination, including those -- is that the totality of the documents that you reviewed in preparation of your report dated approximately March 20th, 2002, including the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did you review?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: There's a very limited selection of the pages of Kozarski Vjesnik, for example, in this collection. I looked at many other pages and articles from Kozarski Vjesnik, from Glas and really, a number of other publications in investigating the election results, the brief section on World War II. There would be, again, a considerable number of additional items that I looked at but did not cite as sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, other than these daily newspaper articles or weekly journals that you may have reviewed, or that you did review, excuse me, that you just mentioned, what other documents did you review in preparation for your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I looked at a number of historical works on World War II in pursuit of specifically what could be attributed to the Prijedor area. I looked at a large number of -- I can't say that I looked at these specifically in preparation for the Prijedor report. But I looked at a large number of interviews and articles and analyses in various magazines from the period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1991 through what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, 1991 through really 1999 or 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have Exhibit S50 in front of you there? I think it's the very last exhibit in that binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, this is an exhibit that was tendered and accepted by the Prosecutor. And briefly I'll just identify it for the Court. It's a letter, dated 15 February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, the witness's report is SK 42. And this would be SK50 only it hasn't been filed officially, so we'll need a copy from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will decide to make all the decisions on the admissability only at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for clarification, I did mention the letter S with the exhibit number, but it was my understanding that it would be, as I stated, S as opposed to SK. Did that change, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to come back to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I just don't want to confuse the record or Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We know what you are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, with respect to Exhibit Number SK 50, that during your direct examination, you were asked: "When was the first time that you were asked to review or analyse the area within Bosnia-Herzegovina identified as Prijedor?" And I believe your response, and this exhibits indicates that the very first time you were asked, sir, to review any materials in connection with Prijedor would have been February 15th, 2002. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If Mr. Ostojic going to cite to what I asked in direct examination, can he give me the page number in the transcript. I've found in the past extremely important to make sure that he accurately characterises what I've asked. If he could point in the transcript to where I asked that question, I'd be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have been faster than me. Of course, please take care and make reference to the transcript. It's available for you, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not. But I would reply with all due respect to the objection if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I personally believe that it's an improper objection. I think that the testimony that was offered on this very limited issue was clear not only to the panel of Judges, I believe, but also to the witness and all the participants. There is no doubt if we changed one word from the Office of the Prosecutor's sentence, all we're trying to do is to expedite this and move forward to see the timetable in which Dr. Donia claims he started to review these materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I fully understand your point. Here, it is more or less a technical question. We all suffer from the TMI -- too much information syndrome. And therefore, when you make reference to the examination-in-chief, please be so kind and quote the page in order that later, we have the possibility to come back to this and really can compare what was said there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To be frank, Your Honour, my learned friend is vigorously objecting because he knows that I never actually asked that question. In fact, the letter was offered as a means of demonstrating to the Court what we had asked Dr. Donia to do. And he knows that very well. So that is why I'm asking him to exercise extreme caution when he suggests that I have asked certain questions, the witness has answered certain questions. And quite frankly, the dates in these particular letters are not as material as he is suggesting. But he's welcome to go on asking questions about these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, it shows that the old Romans were right in saying: What is in the file is in the world. And therefore, it's not only technical but also a substantive question, and I invite once again both parties whenever making reference to a former transcript page, please quote this page, and then it's for the evaluation of the Judges whether or not this was correctly quoted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can state the question a different way, if allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you remember -- strike that. Dr. Donia, am I incorrect if I state that last week during your testimony on direct examination, you stated, sir, according to my notes that the first time you were asked to review and examine and analyse any documents in connection with the Prijedor matter, namely the OTP versus Dr. Stakic was on February 15th, 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't recall making that statement in direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So prior to Exhibit SK50, is it fair to state that prior to February 15th, 2002, you had met with and commenced your review of documents and materials in connection with the Prijedor matter, namely, OTP versus Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on how many occasions prior to February 15th, 2002, did you meet with the Office of the Prosecutor to discuss Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe only once. Now, I must say that the -- Prijedor within the context of the developments in the Bosnian Krajina was a part of my prior report. And consequently, came up, you know, in a number of discussions in terms of preparing that report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the OTP formally retained you as an expert historian on or about February 15th, 2002, or at a subsequent or prior time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I think they formally engaged me on 15 February. But as I say, we talked, had one conversation in January. And I spent about two days looking at documentation in the possession of the OTP in January in the expectation that this letter, this offer, would be formalized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given the documents, sir, to review, or did you ask the Office of the Prosecution for certain documents in order to make your review and analysis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I asked them what they had, and particularly I asked if there were any transcripts or minutes of either party meetings or assembly minutes that might be in the possession of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that the OTP responded to your request for minutes of either party meetings or assembly minutes, correct? They complied with your request?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they gave that to you. Did they, sir, give you the party meeting minutes from the party of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having testified in two prior Croatian cases, do you know, sir, if they're in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your question to the Office of the Prosecutor was broad, from what I can tell. "I want the party meeting minutes for that period in that region" and the Office of the Prosecutor gives you the SDS party minutes and meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I asked for party minutes, and this was on the spur of the moment response, was told we have SDS minutes. And those I then examined over the next 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, forgive me, but you are painting a picture of the region in Bosnia-Herzegovina called Prijedor of the situation as it existed approximately ten years ago. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're trying to enlighten us, to tell us and inform us, essentially to educate us, as to what was going on in that time period at that place. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes. I would only add that it had to be sufficiently economical, that it could not be a comprehensive examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it fair to state that your report and your review of these materials is not comprehensive?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Oh, it certainly is not comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's not thoroughly complete, is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's missing, in your view, of this report, since we now have learned that it's not thoroughly complete?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I think the testimony or account of individuals who were there, witnessed or participated in events. Of this alone, there would be tens of thousands of pages that would fill out this story substantially. I'm sure there are memoirs or personal accounts, diaries. There certainly are the minutes or transcripts of the city -- or the municipal assembly, And minutes or transcripts of not only the HDZ and the SDA, but the reformist party, the SDP, probably the -- if there are such minutes, the short-lived homeland front. All these things would be, I think, required to give a comprehensive picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me understand this: Does the Office of the Prosecutor ask you to review and analyse documents and give a historical background of only the Serbs in the Prijedor area from 1991 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No. As you see, the charge was to identify factors which may have contributed to events in the municipality from April to December 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the very least, the three parties that were in existence in 1990, the SDA, the Muslim majority party; the SDS, the Serbian majority party; and the HDZ, the Croatian majority party, at least those documents would help us to see the entire picture of the area in Prijedor from the period that you're referencing, namely, April 1992 through September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think that more important than those would be probably the documents which actually record the events in the municipal assembly, and the minutes of the non-nationalist parties, which had a totally different role and perspective on events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, those documents would further help us analyse and determine which if any party was reactive or proactive. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say municipal assembly, you're talking about the municipal assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina where, after the elections of 1990, Mr. Izetbegovic was elected. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The municipal assembly to which I'm referring is the Prijedor municipal assembly for which elections were held in November 1990 and which was constituted in the first days of January 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many documents or how many meetings from those municipal assembly meetings from Prijedor have you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I think I've indicated I don't know if they exist. I have not reviewed any of them. I've reviewed the press reports of Kozarski Vjesnik and Glas, which pertain to those meetings as far as I can identify them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you reviewed no such minutes of such an assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, also you never reviewed any of the minutes from the party of the SDA from January 1991 through December 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I'm referencing the party of the SDA, although it spanned the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You didn't review those documents of its governing board, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't review the documents of the local SDA in the Prijedor municipality, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you review any such documents from any other party that had officials or candidates running for office in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to state, sir, that in order to obtain a complete and thorough picture of the area in Prijedor from 1991 through December 1992, one would have to examine those documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: And many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What others would you recommend, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think I've just enumerated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those others --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The -- any diaries or journals that may have been maintained by individuals, any minutes or transcripts of the party of the SP, of the reformist party. And additionally, I think information that might be available from the religious communities, Muslim, Serbian Orthodox, Catholic, and any reports that might be available from outside observers who visited or travelled through the municipality, among others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning again to Exhibit SK50, the February 15th, 2002 letter, if I may, and I ask that you follow along with me, the second full paragraph starts: "Specifically, it is requested that you examine documents in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor which are relevant to the history of the Prijedor municipality." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who determined what documents were relevant to the history of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I think the Office of the Prosecutor representatives and I each rendered judgments on that. I obviously did not get all that I would have liked to have received, but did not know what is in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor regarding some of the other sources. I would add, however, that the substantial bulk of the report is not based at all on documents in the possession of the OTP. It addresses demography; it addresses factors which simply are not of interest to OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that something that they shared with you, that they are not interested in the demographics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just an opinion that you have based on your conversations and discussions with them, that they are not interested in the demographics of that region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No. I think the statement I made was that I examined documents that were not particularly of interest to them in regard to these other issues, and that includes the documents pertaining to demography going back to the 19th century and the other information about -- that I attempted to provide about the revolutionary legacy in Prijedor, and the general environment that existed there in the late socialist period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moments ago, on line 22 of the transcript, you're quoted as saying: "I obviously did not get all that I would have liked to have received," et cetera. Can you tell us, sir, what is it that you would have liked to have receive that you didn't receive?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I'm a -- I think every historian is probably a lover of information and documentation. And I would have loved to have had much more information, but probably could not have included the review of much more for this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask the Office of the Prosecutor for any documents involving the JNA for this time period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that may or may not be relevant in analyzing the situation since you mention and give a history about and reference the JNA, in my opinion, somewhat extensively in your report. Do you think that would assist you in any way in analysing what the role of the JNA was actually in 1991 through 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't share your characterisation of it as extensive. I think it's very brief. And yes, certainly, a great deal of information about the JNA, whether from the archives in Serbia, or the records of the JNA itself, or information from various officers, would have been indeed helpful in providing a more comprehensive picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you think it's more than just helpful, Doctor? Don't you think it's critical in giving and drawing a picture of the events as they existed from 1991 through December 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- it would be important to incorporate it if one could, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not critical, but important. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How important, do you think?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think it would depend on the extent to which one wanted to delve into the specific role of the JNA in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to any police records, or as it has been called, the CZ, Civil Defence, have you reviewed any such documents in connection with the time period that we're discussing here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask for such documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about generally, did you ask for such documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, the general question: "What do you have?" And didn't ask anything more specific than that other than, as I indicated, the request for municipal assembly minutes or SDS party minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's true, in fact, that you did not get invited to the OTP offices and were shown a library of materials and they invited you to go through whatever you deemed relevant. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not given the key to Fort Knox and invited in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, they gave you documents that they wanted you to review and to formulate your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that that was the way their intention was. It was -- specifically, I made a request. They had this body of information and gave it to me. I didn't pursue further information, nor did they say, "Gosh, we found a whole stack of things that we want you to review."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "intention," how would you know someone's intention, whether it be that they wanted to give you the documents or didn't want to give you the documents? How do you make that assessment on someone's intention?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I can't make that assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Our conversation about this was, in fact, very brief, a matter of a minute or two, and went no further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence documents, do you know whether any such TO documents exist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever in any case reviewed any TO documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the SUP? Do you know if documents exist with respect to SUP, which is the police, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any such documents exist relating to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inquire of them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I did not inquire specifically for those documents, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In some portions of your report, perhaps not extensively but you do touch on it, you reference Territorial Defence and you make comments of the movements of the various Territorial Defence groups, if you will. Did you ever ask the Office of the Prosecutor if they were in possession of any documents that may relate to the Territorial Defence, TO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I made the general request, got a body of information which I found, together with the press, to be quite -- both substantial and illuminating. I did not press further for any specific set of records or body of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that in order to discuss, analyse and obtain a complete picture of the events that transpired in Prijedor, from April 1991 -- from April 1992 through December 1992, one must review, examine, analyse, and at the very least be familiar with the very documents that we were previously discussing that you had not reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: To provide a comprehensive account of those developments, I think it's an absolutely essential and an immense task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that it's necessary to have a comprehensive account of those developments if someone is charged serious international crimes by virtue of actions taken by either the individual or in his capacity allegedly as an aider and abettor during that time period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your report is not such a report, is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: It's not such a report, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during your testimony in one of the cases where there were defendants of Croatian ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nationality, thank you. Thank you. Did it involve, in fact, a municipality where a town was called Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that town located?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know what municipality it's in. I think it's in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Konjic municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Konjic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified in connection with the events that occurred on or about April of 1992, or March of 1992, in the Konjic municipality particularly in Celebici. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not testify in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the events that transpired at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: With some, some events, but I can't say I'm intimately familiar with developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that in the Blaskic case, it did or did not involve the municipality and the town that we were just discussing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't recall having made reference in my testimony in Blaskic to Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, sir, remember, as you sit here making reference to the Konjic municipality and the Celebici town in the testimony you gave in January of 2002 in the Brdjanin-Talic matter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't recall a reference to Konjic municipality in that matter, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar that in March or April of 1992, time period we're referencing here, that the Muslim forces in that municipality overtook a military factory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in your report, the addendum you provided to us approximately a month ago, where in that report does it set the stage for us to understand what's going on in Prijedor by telling us that there were these other Muslim forces attacking and seizing military ammunitions factories? Where is it mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, as you know, that was not a part of either the Bosnian Krajina or Prijedor, and my efforts to describe the general situation were extremely brief, both in terms of time and in terms of geographic scope. I believe that no reference is made in either the Krajina or Prijedor report to Konjic municipality or to those events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that's an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We're coming to the well-deserved break, especially for the translators. I would strongly ask both parties to make reference only to the events forming part of the indictment. Of course, it's interesting and, to a certain extent, it may be important to hear other relevant issues from other municipalities, and in other points of time. We have seen the limited request from the side of the Office of the Prosecutor, and we have to be aware that we only should discuss really relevant material here, relevant in the sense also of the substantive criminal law. And that means that already here, we should not start to touch upon the issue of tuquoque. We may now have a break until precisely 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you allow me, first of all, some remarks. When it comes to a question I was asked, and it's only fair from the side of the booth, please wait with the next question until the answer is translated and the other way around. Please pause in between. And the more serious question is, of course, all the parties may all the time be aware that you have a Bench of three professional Judges, and you shouldn't overdo. We immediately can evaluate your points. And then the more technical points are, of course, it's now confirmed by the registry, we'll sit on Friday in the morning. We'll sit as it was said the next -- the days from 1 to 3 May, the entire day. And we will sit the 31st of May, but therefore not on June 3. And not to forget, also right now to have any -- to avoid any kind of misunderstandings, when it is to request 92 bis statements admitted into evidence, one prerequisite is, of course, that, witness by witness, the OTP indicates which statement in the exhibit or in transcript, in which transcript they wanted to tender and request us to admit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, may I just apologise for being a few moments late. Another judge asked to see me on another matter unrelated to this case. As for the 92 bis statements, they actually are being copied and will be filed today with the Court and counsel will get a copy of the requested 92 bis statements. One other brief matter: I had asked the victim witness unit to have the next witness available at 4.00, in case we could get to him. I don't think we're likely to finish before about 6 -- because we have to go through the documents, I don't think we're likely to finish until very late today, if at all. Hopefully we'll finish today but I think it will be late. Does the Court want the witness to standby or shall we excuse him for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's only fair to excuse the witness for the day in order that he, she, has not unnecessary waiting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can that be communicated some way to the outside, to the hall, wherever the witness is, I'm not sure. Or should I walk out and tell him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance. May, in the meantime, Dr. Donia be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue with your leave to cross-examine Dr. Donia, I have a question and would request some clarification on the guidance you were sharing with me and us prior to the last break. And if I may ask that question to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Namely, Your Honour, I would like to confine the questions to the dates in the fourth amended indictment from April 30th, 1992, through September of 1992. However, other witnesses, and in particular Dr. Donia respectfully in his report, has gone beyond those areas. I believe for the Defence in order to show the situation and the tensions that we believe were existing and we believe Dr. Donia concurs were existing at that time in Prijedor, prior to April of 1992, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. through September 1992, is relevant and imperative to obtain both a fair trial for Dr. Stakic and a complete understanding of the situation in that region. And I say this most respectfully, and I'm just looking for guidance. I can limit my questions, but just would like to know if that was the intent of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be very frank on this, I don't know whether counsel, you are aware of the fact that the Trial Chamber already in the beginning asked the Office of the Prosecutor to show us some self-restraint as regards the time covered by this expert witness. And it's not only the time, also the region. Please be aware that we professional Judges regard this as part of, let's say, public domain, that there were overall tensions between the ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia, and therefore, we really should -- all the parties should try to restrict comments and questions on the alleged time, April 1992, September 1992, and of course Prijedor and immediate surrounding areas. This was my point when you came to Celebici, for example. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, very briefly on this matter that you have been referring to and the guidance that my learned friend is looking for, the rules of this institution support you absolutely in what you're saying, and the cross-examination of any witness is to be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness. And that is what you have said. To this moment, I suspect we could, perhaps, broadly interpret Mr. Ostojic's cross-examination as attempting to go to the credibility of the witness, but absolutely no questions have been asked in the last couple of hours on the actual subject matter of what the witness was testifying about. There's nothing been -- there has been nothing directly on the point. And I think equally earlier, you raised the matter of tuquoque, we could of course spend hours cross-examining the witness on what the Muslims were doing, what the Croats were doing, but that's not actually directly relevant to what was happening in Prijedor. So I would only reinforce, Your Honour, what you have already said, that both parties should show some restraint in the manner in which witnesses are examined so that things can be done in a timely and efficient manner. That's all I would add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am compelled to reply, if I may, Your Honour. I take great exception to counsel suggesting that other portions of Bosnia-Herzegovina should not and could not be included, since this expert, this witness, has covered that exhaustively in his report. And I underscore that word particularly because it is our position from the Defence, and I hesitate out of respect for Dr. Donia to say this, but I'm compelled to say it, we believe, and we think we can establish, that it is clearly one-sided. And for us to get to the end gain, if you will, when we start discussing these minutes, unlike what my learned friend said that there is only relevance as it relates to the SDS meetings, for example, which is what he is alluding to, we totally disagree, completely disagree and think that if this witness is going to share with us the events as was requested by the OTP, as he has knowledge and information of, I believe those items in other municipalities are not only relevant, but likewise important for the Defence of Dr. Stakic. If the Court examines the section on the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if you look at his prior exhibit which discusses conversations that Mr. Izetbegovic had with Mr. Milosevic, all that has been accepted at least preliminarily as evidence. All of that, in our view, has to at least be reviewed and analysed to see if it is, again respectfully, distorted or overstated at the very least.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I respond, please. Again, my learned friend has some difficulty in recall what I stated, and I did not state at any time that there is only relevance as it relates to SDS meetings as he well knows. Whilst I accept that questioning cannot be done exclusively on the SDS minutes, there has been some limitation to the scope of cross-examination. And I am simply relying on the rules. The rules of this institution, Rule 90 [H] (i) state cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of evidence-in-chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness. My learned friend can be allowed to broadly go across every region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the re-examination will be extensive if that is allowed, Your Honour. I also think, as you've reminded Mr. Ostojic already, he is not pleading to a jury. There are three professional Judges sitting on the Bench, and that I think is an important consideration in all of this, in the manner in which this cross-examination is conducted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To conclude, I think I was quite clear in saying we have only a limited time of responsibility at stake here in our case. You know this time, and you know the region. Of course, you can go to the surrounding areas. This is of some importance. But it was on purpose that I asked both parties in the beginning not to start history with the tribes in the 5th and 6th century. It doesn't make sense at all. And I said it quite clearly to the Office of the Prosecutor and the same is of course true for the Defence. And therefore, I have to ask you, concentrate yourselves first of all on this limited time and the limited area. And please, allow me one additional remark: As this is not a jury, I, as a Defence counsel, have always learned that it's more convincing to make some points and leave the evaluation to the Judges. Thank you. I think it's enough, and we should continue with the cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, would you agree with me that the tensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly the Prijedor municipality, were accelerating as the months went on from 1991 to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Certainly from 1991 into the summer of 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you, sir, have an opinion as to what the causes of the acceleration of those tensions were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
