I believe that they are trying to make it greater than it is. We'll discuss that at a later time. But I don't think there's a need for this questioning on this and this distortion, based upon what one individual said purportedly, written by another party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think your contribution is only fair, and please proceed. I don't think it's really relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't wish me to ask any more questions on this, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not on this special question, as you put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, based on what Mr. Safic here states, do you believe that the SDS had a genuine desire to cooperate on a bona fides basis in the work of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, my learned friend has gone through these minutes and asked a number of questions in similar fashion, and now all I'm asking from the witness, since this is a matter that my learned friend actually raised with the witness himself, whether or not this particular statement by this individual represents a genuine desire on behalf of the SDS to cooperate in the municipal assembly. It's a reasonable question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed, I agree with your view.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: My feeling is it did not represent at this point a genuine desire to cooperate. And that's not simply the vote and statement taken here regarding obstruction, but also the press release that was issued on the 18th, which is discussed in these minutes. And the concurrent -- roughly concurrent -- walkout from the executive committee and these events are all discussed in the minutes of this meeting and, in the context at looking at all of them, I think becomes clear that this was not a genuine desire to continue the process of seeking a cooperative solution to the issues facing the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you were asked a number of questions at the commencement of your cross-examination about the cases that you've testified in before the Tribunal. You stated that you testified in a case where the accused was a Bosnian Croat; you stated that you testified in a case where the accused was a Bosnian Serb. You also stated that you had not testified in any case where there was a Bosnian Muslim accused. If you were requested to give evidence in such a case, in a case with a Bosnian Muslim accused, would you consider giving expert evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of your testimony, you were asked about your opinion on the accuracy of these minutes. Were you able to corroborate the accuracy of these minutes from your knowledge of events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Krajina generally during the period of these minutes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the best method to validate any given source, is to do so in light of information that occurs in other sources, reflecting the same events or dealing with the same time. And that is, I think, the basis on which I assessed these minutes and the various press reports and other documents pertaining to events that are discussed in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that basis, on your knowledge of events within Prijedor, within the Krajina, within Bosnia-Herzegovina, during the period of these minutes, how accurate would you say these minutes are as to how they reflect contemporary events at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think they are generally accurate. Obviously not as complete as one would like to have them, such as might be derived from a transcript. But their general references or the references to events here are in many, many cases reflected in other documents referring to the same events. So I would view this as -- these minutes as accurate to a reasonably high level of ability to verify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've finished my re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. There are some additional questions. In order that it is not regarded as unfair from the side of the Defence, I want to come back explicitly at 16.53.36. There was still one question open. I asked you, Dr. Donia, to come back to this question after the break. And there was a question from the Defence: "Is there any concrete evidence, sir, that the SDS party formed an entity such as the Bosnian Muslim Green Berets, a paramilitary unit, in the Prijedor municipality?" Did you take the opportunity of the break to come back to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not have the documents to make reference to. I am simply not able to give you what I'm looking for in a brief period of time. I would, I guess -- let me not say any more than that. I think the declarations that I'm looking for, I can't put my hands on in a very -- in a very brief period of time. But I would, perhaps, clarify that if the question goes to the formation of a paramilitary organisation on the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I don't believe that such a decision was undertaken by the SDS at any time up until May 12th, 1992. But there were numerous decisions to mobilise local units, gather volunteers, and recruit volunteers or reservists for police units which functioned in a capacity that I would say is very parallel to the operation of the two units of the -- organised by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Another question. The basis for this question is first of all to avoid the admission of unnecessary additional evidence from your former statements. The question was raised whether or not you had enough time for the preparation of your separate opinion on the situation in Prijedor. Did you, in the preparation of former statements, especially in the case of OTP versus Brdjanin/Talic, touch upon the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you take this into account when preparing the part we have before us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When were you asked to prepare your representation for Brdjanin/Talic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Sometime in the fall of last year, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One other question: When have you been the last time in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: February of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When have you been the last time in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: February of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have access to documents there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I did not seek access and did not have any, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not in the past, not before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Try to get access to archives, be it in Prijedor, or be it in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I've never worked in any of the regional archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so I have not sought documents nor been given them in the regional archive in Banja Luka, nor any of the smaller towns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this assistance. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Would you please be a little more explicit, elaborate, on the association that you created, this foundation, yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] What is its purpose?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The foundation was established for the purpose of using the limited charitable donations of myself and my family to support educational and development activities in the former Yugoslavia, or relating to the former Yugoslavia, principally Bosnia. Since these donations all must go through another charitable organisation, there's a very limited ability to do projects. The vast majority of the funds have gone to the University of Michigan, which has an ongoing series of projects relating to the former Yugoslavia; the St. Lawrence University, which has a solidarity project, devoted to the supporting publication of scholarly works and support for young professionals in Bosnia; and a group called the Business Development Initiative, which organised a programme to bring young business professors from Banja Luka, Mostar, and Sarajevo, to a programme of entrepreneurship in Silicon Valley. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] So it's by pure chance that you choose that particular name for your foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, at the time I liked the pun on the name of the municipality. I've since grown to like it less. But yes, it was a whim to choose that name. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Because apparently, the name means "religious donation" or "foundation"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: The term means "support for a religious or educational institution" of some Islamic nature, yes. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Precisely. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, as a historian, a scholar, can you clarify whether Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina is ethnic or religious group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: It is a ethnonational community, nationality. And by that I mean an ethnic group. It is distinguished -- let me pause and ask if you have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: In this regard, what are the native or mother languages of the Muslim and Serbs living in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: There has historically been no real distinction among the languages. However, in the last, let's say, 15 years, there has been attempt by intellectual elites to define these languages as increasingly separate, Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you speak those languages?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what is Bosnian language for "country"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: "Zemlja".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: I guess "Zemlja".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Not "Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: "Krajina" means "border land" or "boundary area".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And probably my last question is the following: Do you actually exercise any other profession?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be quite clear, because we had these questions but without a very precise solution, until when -- or better, since when would you say do you exercise the profession as historian alone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Since September of 1998, I have not been actively committed to working for Merrill Lynch, actively engaged in day-to-day work for Merrill Lynch since then. And that would be the time I would say I have been fully engaged as an historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before that, more or less, as on a good background, of course, as a hobby historian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I, I think, had a brief but good career until 1981. And when I joined Merrill Lynch, I devoted less and less time to either following literature and certainly to writing. It's true that publications of mine continued to come out for another six years. And in 1993, I was able to take enough time away from work to begin writing historical work again. But really, not time to do extensive research. So really, only since September of 1998 have I been working full time as a historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Could we, then, please try to proceed on the first documents we have only available in B/C/S in order to demonstrate or to give the OTP a chance to demonstrate whether or not it's really necessary to tender this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated to you, I believe that all of the newspaper articles which Dr. Donia has marked are relevant in terms of a record of the evidence in this case, because he relies upon them in his report. He has identified in each of those newspaper articles the portion relevant for translation. So where you have a newspaper article with five or six articles in it, he has basically highlighted with a yellow highlighter, the particular section. In a sense, because I can't read the language, it's probably better if you actually ask him why the particular document is relevant. And equally, as I know you made the point in terms of public money last time and the time it takes to translate this, I think we have abbreviated the translation process by going through all of the documents and marking the yellow part. The only thing we haven't got is the agreement from the Defence to whether or not they wish to have additional parts translated, because they were unable to meet with us on Tuesday. So I don't know if you would wish to hear representations from them on that issue, as to whether they want additional parts translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's just have one example: SK1, if the usher could please put this on the ELMO. SK1. Would you please, so that we have an idea, read out the portions you marked in yellow.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This, if I may just identify it, is an article reporting on a speech by a member of the Partisan Veterans' Association recalling in his version the events of 1941. And I guess I'll have to -- this is an exercise in micro-history as well by virtue of the size of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a document from 6 September, 1991. Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] "The anniversary of the Karan battalion celebrated with a magnificent gathering of people attended by several thousand citizens of Prijedor, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanski Novi municipalities on Sunday celebrating the 90th anniversary of the establishment of the Karan battalion. 'We must never forget', continued Baskut, 'that in the Karan battalion as well as in other places, in the first days of insurgency, together with Serbs, numerous sons of the Muslims, Croat, and Jewish people fought back to back, and these fighters of the national liberation struggle were joined by Muslims in ever-greater numbers.' 'We must also not forget,' Baskut emphasised, 'that the fighters of the NOB, the national liberation struggle, had to fight beginning with 1942 the Chetniks of Draza Mihajlovic as well because of their collaboration with the occupator and the Ustashas.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for providing us with this example. And I think it's now for the next hearing that we go on discussing page by page whether this excerpt from a newspaper as such is really relevant and whether it's really necessary to have the document as such, and not only the report, including this material. But I really believe it would not be possible to do this today, and therefore I would say we should proceed tomorrow. But I don't regard it as necessary to have the assistance of the Dr. Donia on all the documents. Do the parties agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The problem is, Your Honour, is in actually justifying the relevance of the particular article. The reason that these are offered in evidence is because they are the newspaper reports referred to in the foot notes. So for example, this one that he has just read out, it is a newspaper report that is cited to in his report and supports an assertion that he is making. I think we do need him here, particularly if you are asking questions about whether or not it's relevant. Because I cannot read the language. I can read it a little bit in Latin script, but certainly not in Cyrillic script, so I think the quickest way to do this is to have Dr. Donia here, with respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I have the view of the Defence on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, briefly looking through these documents, I saw that the Defence would mark completely different parts of the document. And I can read it to you loudly. So I don't think that we need Dr. Donia. I don't think that he should bother with us if we want to translate something or not. Maybe we should work it together with the Bench or the Prosecutor. So I think that marked portions of this text do not depict the real message from the speech of this speaker. If you want, I can read the other portions which will depict the real message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's revisit this issue tomorrow. And if the parties so agree -- please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, this was the whole purpose of the meeting yesterday, was to achieve exactly what Mr. Lukic is saying, that we would have sat down together. We mark the portions that we wanted translated. He could mark the portions that he wanted translated, and then we wouldn't now be in the position of having to do it in the courtroom. But that meeting, for whatever reason, I don't know why, was not possible. And it's my view that the quickest way to do this is in essence for Your Honours to admit all of these documents and for the relevant portions marked by Dr. Donia and the relevant portions marked by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Lukic and Mr. Ostojic as being required to be translated into English and French, for Your Honours to review. Otherwise, I think we are going to be here literally for hours and hours and hours going through these documents with Dr. Donia present. I mean, I think it's going to take the best part of a session to go through it. And Mr. Koumjian is whispering in my ear that there are two witnesses that are waiting that he doesn't want to send back to Bosnia. I mean, I could -- sorry, if I might just finish. I could get together with Mr. Lukic, with the copy that Dr. Donia has which he's marked, and Mr. Lukic can mark up that copy, the parts that he wants to be translated into English and French, and then we can simply offer the documents to the Court and have them admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be possible for the parties to meet tomorrow in the morning, that we can decide on this in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm available as well. But as you know, Your Honour, I have to mention that we were sitting in the trial yesterday, so that's why I couldn't show up in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I think here it's not necessary to apologise for this. I really appreciate your spirit of cooperation. And I expect that we hear the results of your meeting tomorrow very brief in the beginning in order to continue with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it would be wise if Dr. Donia was present at that meeting with the parties. Then, he can confirm the parts that he wants translated, and I think hopefully we'll be able to return to you tomorrow, Your Honours, with agreed documents that I will apply for admission into evidence and hopefully we will deal with any potential objections they may have over any documents. We can also deal with that at the meeting and come to some kind of agreement

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is this agreed in order not to have a contract, yes, against you? You're also prepared to participate in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's proceed this way, and it shouldn't take more than 20, maximum 30 minutes to continue this discussion, and then we can proceed with our witness. The trial stays adjourned. We resume tomorrow afternoon.
